title: How a DNA-PAINT image is made
caption: First the whole 55 um field (the average of early raw frames) with the region that follows boxed; then that 1.7 um region at the diffraction limit, where each DNA origami is a single blurred spot. Next, raw frames (0.3 s each) in which dye-labelled imager strands bind briefly to docking strands on the origami, beside the image building up from the localisations of every frame so far; in the first frames cyan rings mark the binding events localised in the frame shown. After 40,000 frames each origami (about 90 x 70 nm, a 6 x 8 grid of sites) appears as a cluster of binding sites; the movie ends on a zoom of a triangle, one of the 'sharp triangle' origami the study mixed in as fiducial markers. The raw frames are not drift-corrected, so the reconstruction is drawn where the camera saw each molecule at that moment and drifts with the stage (about 0.4 um in x and 0.6 um in y over the 3.3-hour recording). From the team's digital nucleic acid memory study: DNA-PAINT in TIRF, Nikon Ti2, 100x/1.49 plus 1.5x, 561 nm, ProEM EMCCD; the movie samples the recording, every frame at first and then faster.
paper: Dickinson GD, Mortuza GM, Clay W, et al. (2021) An alternative approach to nucleic acid memory. Nat Commun 12:2371
evidence: Published open data (Zenodo 4672665, MIT licence; paper CC BY 4.0). Raw frames and the study's own ThunderSTORM localisations, drift-corrected in Picasso. The stage drift was measured back for display: per segment of the recording, the shift of the localisations that maximises the raw intensity under them (residual under 0.25 camera px after correction). Display only.
